title: Moving Charges & Magnetism
subtitle: Zero-to-JEE-Advanced Visual Textbook: Biot-Savart Law, Straight Wire & Circular Loop Fields, Ampere's Circuital Law, Solenoid & Toroid, Lorentz Force, Circular & Helical Motion, Cyclotron, Parallel Wire Forces, Magnetic Dipole Torque & Moving-Coil Galvanometer
introduction:
💡 First-Time Reader Intuition: How Do Moving Charges Create Magnetism?

For thousands of years, electricity and magnetism were thought to be two completely unrelated forces of nature. In 1820, Hans Christian Oersted noticed that a compass needle placed near a wire deflected violently the moment an electric current was switched on! Why?

While a stationary charge ($v = 0$) produces only an Electric Field ($\vec{E}$) in the space around it, a moving charge ($v \neq 0$, or an electric current $I$) produces BOTH an Electric Field ($\vec{E}$) and a Magnetic Field ($\vec{B}$)! Furthermore, a magnetic field exerts a force only on moving charges—never on a stationary charge.

SI & CGS Units of Magnetic Field ($\vec{B}$, also called Magnetic Flux Density):
  • SI Unit: $1\text{ Tesla (T)} = 1\text{ Weber/m}^2\text{ (Wb/m}^2\text{)} = 1\text{ N}\cdot\text{A}^{-1}\text{m}^{-1}$.
  • CGS Unit: $1\text{ Gauss (G)}$, where $\boxed{1\text{ Tesla} = 10^4\text{ Gauss} \iff 1\text{ G} = 10^{-4}\text{ T}}$.
  • Dimensions of $\vec{B}$: From $F = I L B$, $\boxed{[B] = [M^1 L^0 T^{-2} A^{-1}]}$.

topics.title: Biot-Savart Law & Magnetic Field of Straight Wires, Circular Arcs, Rings & Axial Coils
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 Biot-Savart Law (Current Element & Moving Point Charge Forms)
Statement & Right-Hand Thumb Rule:
The tiny magnetic field $d\vec{B}$ at position $\vec{r}$ produced by a small current element $I\,d\vec{\ell}$ is perpendicular to both $d\vec{\ell}$ and $\vec{r}$ (point your right thumb along current $I$; your curled fingers give the circular direction of $\vec{B}$):
$$\text{Current Element Form:} \qquad \boxed{d\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I(d\vec{\ell} \times \hat{r})}{r^2} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I(d\vec{\ell} \times \vec{r})}{r^3}} \qquad \implies \qquad dB = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,d\ell\sin\theta}{r^2}$$
$$\text{Moving Point Charge Form } (I\,d\vec{\ell} \to q\vec{v}): \qquad \boxed{\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{q(\vec{v} \times \hat{r})}{r^2} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{q(\vec{v} \times \vec{r})}{r^3}}$$

Where $\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} = 10^{-7}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}$ (so permeability of free space is $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}$), and $\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}} = c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$.

1.2 Master Dictionary of Magnetic Fields ($\vec{B}$) for Wires, Loops & Polygons
Current-Carrying GeometryPoint LocationMaster Magnetic Field Formula
1. Point on the Line of a Straight Wire
($\theta = 0^\circ$ or $180^\circ$)		Anywhere along the extended axis of the wire$$\boxed{B = 0} \quad (\text{since } d\vec{\ell} \parallel \vec{r} \implies \sin 0^\circ = 0)$$
2. Finite Straight Wire
(Perpendicular distance $d$, end angles $\theta_1, \theta_2$)		At perpendicular distance $d$$$\boxed{B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}(\sin\theta_1 + \sin\theta_2)}$$
3. Infinite Straight Wire ($\theta_1 = \theta_2 = 90^\circ$)At perpendicular distance $d$$$\boxed{B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}} \qquad \left(\text{Semi-Infinite Wire } (\theta_1=90^\circ, \theta_2=0^\circ): \; \boxed{B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}}\right)$$
4. Circular Arc subtending Angle $\alpha$ (in rad)At center of curvature $O$ (radius $R$)$$\boxed{B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R}\alpha} \qquad \left(\text{Full Circle } \alpha = 2\pi: \; \boxed{B_{\text{center}} = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}}\right)$$
5. Circular Coil on Axis
($N$ turns, radius $R$, axial distance $x$)		On axis at distance $x$ from center$$\boxed{B_{\text{axis}}(x) = \frac{\mu_0 N I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}} \qquad \left(\text{For } x \gg R: \; B \approx \frac{\mu_0 (N I \pi R^2)}{2\pi x^3} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2\mu}{x^3}\right)$$
6. Regular Polygon of $n$ Sides (Inscribed circle radius $d$, or side $a$)At geometric center$$\boxed{B = \frac{n \mu_0 I}{2\pi d}\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{n}\right) = \frac{n \mu_0 I}{\pi a}\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{n}\right)\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{n}\right)}$$
(Square of side $a$: $B = \frac{2\sqrt{2}\mu_0 I}{\pi a}$; Equilateral triangle of side $a$: $B = \frac{9\mu_0 I}{2\pi a}$)
topics.derivationHtml:
Calculus Derivation 1: Finite Straight Wire B = (μ₀I / 4πd)(sin θ₁ + sin θ₂)

Let point $P$ be at perpendicular distance $d$ from a straight wire carrying current $I$. Take an element $dy$ at distance $y = d\tan\theta$ from the foot of the perpendicular (so $dy = d\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$, $r = d\sec\theta$, and angle between $d\vec{y}$ and $\vec{r}$ is $90^\circ - \theta$):

$$B = \int_{-\theta_2}^{+\theta_1} \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi}\frac{(d\sec^2\theta\,d\theta)\cos\theta}{(d\sec\theta)^2} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}\int_{-\theta_2}^{+\theta_1} \cos\theta\,d\theta = \boxed{\frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}(\sin\theta_1 + \sin\theta_2)}$$
Calculus Derivation 2: Circular Loop on Axis B = μ₀ I R² / [2(R² + x²)^(3/2)]

At axial distance $x$ from the center of a circular ring of radius $R$, every element $d\ell$ is at distance $r = \sqrt{R^2 + x^2}$ and perpendicular to $\vec{r}$ ($dB = \frac{\mu_0 I\,d\ell}{4\pi(R^2 + x^2)}$). Radial components $dB\cos\phi$ cancel out by symmetry, while axial components $dB\sin\phi$ (where $\sin\phi = \frac{R}{\sqrt{R^2 + x^2}}$) add around the circumference $\oint d\ell = 2\pi R$:

$$B_{\text{axis}} = \oint dB\sin\phi = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi(R^2 + x^2)}\left(\frac{R}{\sqrt{R^2 + x^2}}\right)(2\pi R) = \boxed{\frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Universal Zero-Field Rule for Any Closed Loop of Uniform Wire): If current $I$ enters ANY symmetric or asymmetric closed loop made of uniform resistance wire (circle, square, triangle) at point $A$ and leaves at point $B$, dividing into paths $(L_1, R_1)$ and $(L_2, R_2)$, then since $I_1 R_1 = I_2 R_2 \implies I_1 L_1 = I_2 L_2$, the clockwise and counter-clockwise magnetic fields at the center ALWAYS cancel out to EXACTLY ZERO ($B_{\text{center}} = 0$)!
  • Trap 2 (Angles $\theta_1, \theta_2$ in Finite Wire Formula): In $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}(\sin\theta_1 + \sin\theta_2)$, $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ are measured from the perpendicular line $d$ at point $P$! If the question gives the angles $\alpha, \beta$ made with the wire itself, use $\boxed{B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}(\cos\alpha + \cos\beta)}$ (or $\cos\alpha - \cos\beta$ if both ends lie on the same side of the foot of the perpendicular)!

topics.title: Ampere's Circuital Law, Solid & Hollow Cylindrical Conductors, Solenoid, Toroid & Infinite Current Sheet
topics.theoryHtml:
2.1 Ampere's Circuital Law
Statement:
The line integral of the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ around any closed loop (Amperian loop) in free space is equal to $\mu_0$ times the net algebraic electric current $I_{\text{enclosed}}$ threading (piercing through) the area bounded by the loop:
$$\boxed{\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = \mu_0 I_{\text{enclosed}}}$$

Right-Hand Sign Rule for $I_{\text{enclosed}}$: Curl the fingers of your right hand along the direction of integration around the Amperian loop; currents piercing the loop in the direction of your outstretched thumb are taken as positive ($+I$), and opposite currents as negative ($-I$).

2.2 Master Magnetic Field Results from Ampere's Law
Symmetric Current DistributionInside ($r < R$)Outside ($r \ge R$)
1. Hollow Cylindrical Pipe
(Current $I$ on surface only)		$$\boxed{B_{\text{in}} = 0}$$$$\boxed{B_{\text{out}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}}$$
2. Solid Cylindrical Wire
(Uniform current density $J = \frac{I}{\pi R^2}$)		$$\boxed{B_{\text{in}} = \frac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi R^2} = \frac{1}{2}\mu_0 J r} \quad (B \propto r)$$$$\boxed{B_{\text{out}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}} \quad \left(B \propto \frac{1}{r}\right)$$
3. Cylindrical Cavity Inside Solid Wire
(Current density $\vec{J}$, center shift $\vec{d} = \vec{O_1 O_2}$)		Uniform Magnetic Field Everywhere Inside the Cavity!
$$\boxed{\vec{B}_{\text{cavity}} = \frac{1}{2}\mu_0 (\vec{J} \times \vec{d}) \implies B_{\text{cavity}} = \frac{1}{2}\mu_0 J d}$$
4. Finite & Long Solenoid
($n = \frac{N}{L} =$ turns per unit length)		• General Axis Point: $\boxed{B = \frac{\mu_0 n I}{2}(\cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2)}$
• Deep Inside Long Solenoid: $\boxed{B_{\text{center}} = \mu_0 n I}$
• At Either End of Long Solenoid: $\boxed{B_{\text{end}} = \frac{1}{2}\mu_0 n I}$		$B_{\text{outside ideal solenoid}} \approx 0$
5. Toroid (Endless Circular Solenoid)
(Total turns $N$, mean radius $r$)		Inside core: $$\boxed{B = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2\pi r} = \mu_0 n I}$$$B = 0$ in empty central hole AND outside!
6. Infinite Flat Current Sheet
($K =$ linear current density in $\text{A/m}$)		$$\boxed{B = \frac{1}{2}\mu_0 K} \quad (\text{Uniform, parallel to sheet, independent of distance!})$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Ampere's Law Proof for Inside a Solid Cylindrical Wire (r < R) & Cavity Superposition

1. Inside Solid Cylinder ($r < R$): Draw a circular Amperian loop of radius $r < R$ concentric with the wire axis. The current enclosed within area $\pi r^2$ is $I_{\text{enc}} = J(\pi r^2) = I\left(\frac{\pi r^2}{\pi R^2}\right) = I\frac{r^2}{R^2}$. Applying Ampere's Law:

$$\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 \left(I\frac{r^2}{R^2}\right) \implies \boxed{B_{\text{in}}(r) = \frac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi R^2} = \frac{1}{2}\mu_0 J r}$$

2. Vector Form & Cavity Proof: In vector form, $\vec{B}_{\text{in}}(\vec{r}) = \frac{1}{2}\mu_0 (\vec{J} \times \vec{r})$. By superposing a full cylinder ($+\vec{J}$ at $O_1$) and a negative cylinder ($-\vec{J}$ at $O_2$, with $\vec{r}_1 - \vec{r}_2 = \vec{d}$), the field inside the cavity is $\vec{B}_{\text{cavity}} = \frac{1}{2}\mu_0 \vec{J} \times (\vec{r}_1 - \vec{r}_2) = \boxed{\frac{1}{2}\mu_0 (\vec{J} \times \vec{d}) = \text{Constant}}$!

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Solenoid End Field Is Half of Center Field): At the exact open end of a long solenoid, one end subtends $\theta_1 = 90^\circ$ ($\cos 90^\circ = 0$) and the far end subtends $\theta_2 = 0^\circ$ ($\cos 0^\circ = 1$), so $\boxed{B_{\text{end}} = \frac{1}{2}\mu_0 n I = \frac{1}{2}B_{\text{center}}}$!

topics.title: Magnetic Lorentz Force, Zero-Work Theorem, Circular & Helical Trajectories, Wall Boundary Deviation, Cyclotron & Velocity Selector
topics.theoryHtml:
3.1 Magnetic Force on a Moving Charge & The Zero-Work Theorem
$$\text{Magnetic Force:} \quad \boxed{\vec{F}_m = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B}) \implies F_m = |q| v B \sin\theta} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{Total Lorentz Force:} \quad \boxed{\vec{F} = q\vec{E} + q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})}$$
Why a Static Magnetic Field Can NEVER Change the Speed or Kinetic Energy of a Particle:
Because the cross product $\vec{F}_m = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$ is ALWAYS strictly perpendicular to velocity $\vec{v}$, instantaneous power delivered by a magnetic force is identically zero: $$\boxed{P = \vec{F}_m \cdot \vec{v} = 0 \implies W_{\text{magnetic}} = \Delta K = 0 \implies |\vec{v}| = \text{Constant!}}$$A magnetic field can only deflect the direction of velocity (changing momentum $\vec{p}$), never its speed or kinetic energy!
3.2 Trajectory of a Charged Particle in a Uniform Magnetic Field $\vec{B}$

Case 1: $\theta = 0^\circ$ or $180^\circ$ ($\vec{v} \parallel \vec{B}$): $\vec{F}_m = 0 \implies$ Straight line with constant velocity.
Case 2: $\theta = 90^\circ$ ($\vec{v} \perp \vec{B}$ — Uniform Circular Motion): Equating magnetic force $qvB$ to centripetal force $\frac{mv^2}{R}$:

$$\boxed{R = \frac{m v}{q B} = \frac{p}{q B} = \frac{\sqrt{2 m K}}{q B} = \frac{\sqrt{2 m q V_{\text{acc}}}}{q B} = \frac{1}{B}\sqrt{\frac{2 m V_{\text{acc}}}{q}}}$$
$$\text{Time Period:} \quad \boxed{T = \frac{2\pi R}{v} = \frac{2\pi m}{q B}}, \qquad \text{Cyclotron Frequency:} \quad \boxed{f = \frac{q B}{2\pi m}}, \qquad \text{Angular Speed:} \quad \boxed{\omega = \frac{q B}{m}}$$

Crucial Insight: Time period $T = \frac{2\pi m}{qB}$ and frequency $f$ are 100% INDEPENDENT of particle speed $v$ and radius $R$! (A faster particle simply traces a proportionally larger circle in the exact same time $T$—the principle of the Cyclotron, where $K_{\max} = \frac{q^2 B^2 R_{\text{dee}}^2}{2m}$).

Case 3: Oblique Entry ($\theta \neq 0^\circ, 90^\circ, 180^\circ$ — Helical Path / Helix):
Resolve $\vec{v}$ into $v_{\parallel} = v\cos\theta$ (along $\vec{B}$, unaffected) and $v_{\perp} = v\sin\theta$ (perpendicular to $\vec{B}$, causes circular motion):

$$\text{Helix Radius:} \quad \boxed{R = \frac{m v_{\perp}}{q B} = \frac{m v \sin\theta}{q B}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{Pitch (Axial advance per period } T\text{):} \quad \boxed{p_{\text{pitch}} = v_{\parallel} T = \frac{2\pi m v \cos\theta}{q B}}$$

Case 4: Crossed Electric & Magnetic Fields ($\vec{E} \perp \vec{B} \perp \vec{v}$ — Velocity Selector):
For zero net deflection ($q\vec{E} + q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B}) = 0$), only particles with speed $\boxed{v = \frac{E}{B}}$ pass straight through!
topics.derivationHtml:
Particle Entering a Magnetic Wall Region of Width d (Angular Deviation & Time Spent)

Suppose a particle of mass $m$, charge $q$, and speed $v$ enters perpendicularly ($\theta = 90^\circ$) into a magnetic field strip of width $d$ (circular radius $R = \frac{mv}{qB}$):

1. If $d < R$ (Particle exits the far side): By geometry, $\boxed{\sin\theta = \frac{d}{R} = \frac{qBd}{mv}}$. Angular deviation is $\theta = \arcsin\left(\frac{d}{R}\right)$, and time spent inside the field is $t = \frac{\theta}{\omega} = \frac{m\theta}{qB}$.

2. If $d \ge R$ (Particle CANNOT cross the strip!): It completes a full semicircle ($\Delta\theta = \pi = 180^\circ$) and exits back through the entry boundary after spending time $\boxed{t = \frac{T}{2} = \frac{\pi m}{qB}}$!

• Trap (Comparing Proton $p$, Deuteron $d$, and Alpha Particle $\alpha$ Radii in the Same $\vec{B}$):
    Masses are $m_p : m_d : m_\alpha = 1 : 2 : 4$ and charges are $q_p : q_d : q_\alpha = 1 : 1 : 2$.
    • Same Speed $v$ ($R \propto \frac{m}{q}$): $R_p : R_d : R_\alpha = \frac{1}{1} : \frac{2}{1} : \frac{4}{2} = \mathbf{1 : 2 : 2}$.
    • Same Momentum $p$ ($R \propto \frac{1}{q}$): $R_p : R_d : R_\alpha = \frac{1}{1} : \frac{1}{1} : \frac{1}{2} = \mathbf{2 : 2 : 1}$.
    • Same Kinetic Energy $K$ ($R \propto \frac{\sqrt{m}}{q}$): $R_p : R_d : R_\alpha = \frac{1}{1} : \frac{\sqrt{2}}{1} : \frac{2}{2} = \mathbf{1 : \sqrt{2} : 1}$.
    • Same Accelerating Voltage $V$ ($R \propto \sqrt{\frac{m}{q}}$): $R_p : R_d : R_\alpha = 1 : \sqrt{2} : \sqrt{2}$!

topics.title: Force on Current-Carrying Wires, Parallel Wires, Magnetic Dipole Moment, Gyromagnetic Ratio, Torque & Moving-Coil Galvanometer
topics.theoryHtml:
4.1 Magnetic Force on a Current-Carrying Wire & Parallel Wires
Effective Vector Length Shortcut in a Uniform Magnetic Field $\vec{B}$:
For ANY arbitrarily curved wire carrying current $I$ from starting point $A$ to endpoint $B$ inside a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$, the total magnetic force depends ONLY on the straight displacement vector $\vec{L}_{\text{eff}} = \vec{AB}$ joining its two ends!
$$\boxed{\vec{F} = I\left(\int_A^B d\vec{\ell}\right) \times \vec{B} = I(\vec{L}_{\text{eff}} \times \vec{B})} \qquad \implies \qquad \textbf{Closed Current Loop in Uniform } \vec{B}: \; \boxed{\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = 0}$$

Force per Unit Length Between Two Parallel Infinite Wires Separated by Distance $d$:

$$\boxed{\frac{F}{L} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}} \qquad \begin{cases} \textbf{Parallel Currents (Same Direction):} & \text{ATTRACT each other!} \\ \textbf{Antiparallel Currents (Opposite Direction):} & \text{REPEL each other!} \end{cases}$$
4.2 Magnetic Dipole Moment ($\vec{\mu}$ or $\vec{M}$), Gyromagnetic Ratio & Torque in Uniform $\vec{B}$
$$\text{Current Loop of } N \text{ Turns & Area } \vec{A}: \qquad \boxed{\vec{\mu} = N I \vec{A}} \qquad (\text{SI Unit: } \text{A}\cdot\text{m}^2 = \text{J/T})$$
Universal Gyromagnetic Ratio ($\frac{\mu}{L} = \frac{q}{2m}$):
For ANY uniformly charged body (orbiting electron, rotating ring, spinning solid disk, or solid/hollow sphere) where charge $q$ and mass $m$ are distributed in the exact same spatial proportion, the ratio of its Magnetic Dipole Moment ($\mu$) to its Angular Momentum ($L$) is a universal constant:
$$\boxed{\frac{\mu}{L} = \frac{q}{2m} \implies \vec{\mu} = \left(\frac{q}{2m}\right)\vec{L} = \left(\frac{q}{2m}\right)I_{\text{MI}}\vec{\omega}}$$

For a Bohr Hydrogen Electron ($L = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$): $\mu_n = \frac{e}{2m_e}\left(\frac{nh}{2\pi}\right) = n\,\mu_B$, where Bohr Magneton $\mu_B = \frac{eh}{4\pi m_e} = 9.27 \times 10^{-24}\text{ A}\cdot\text{m}^2$.

$$\textbf{Torque in Uniform } \vec{B}: \quad \boxed{\vec{\tau} = \vec{\mu} \times \vec{B} = \mu B \sin\theta} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \textbf{Potential Energy:} \quad \boxed{U(\theta) = -\vec{\mu}\cdot\vec{B} = -\mu B \cos\theta}$$

Moving-Coil Galvanometer (Radial Magnetic Field $\theta = 90^\circ \implies \sin\theta = 1$):
Equating magnetic deflecting torque $N I A B$ to torsional restoring torque $k\phi$ gives linear scale deflection $\boxed{\phi = \left(\frac{NAB}{k}\right)I}$:
• Current Sensitivity: $S_I = \frac{\phi}{I} = \frac{NAB}{k}$.
• Voltage Sensitivity: $S_V = \frac{\phi}{V} = \frac{\phi}{I R_G} = \frac{NAB}{k R_G} = \frac{S_I}{R_G}$.
topics.derivationHtml:
Proof of Gyromagnetic Ratio μ / L = q / (2m) & Ring Tension I B R

1. Gyromagnetic Ratio Proof: A particle of charge $q$ and mass $m$ orbiting in a circle of radius $r$ at speed $v$ constitutes current $I = \frac{qv}{2\pi r}$. Its magnetic moment is $\mu = I(\pi r^2) = \frac{qvr}{2}$, while its angular momentum is $L = mvr$. Dividing the two immediately gives $\boxed{\frac{\mu}{L} = \frac{qvr / 2}{mvr} = \frac{q}{2m}}$! Because any symmetric rotating body is a sum of concentric rings, this ratio holds for rods, disks, shells, and solid spheres!

2. Hoop Tension in a Circular Current Loop of Radius $R$ Placed in Perpendicular $\vec{B}$: Take a small top arc of angle $2d\theta$ (length $2R\,d\theta$). Outward magnetic force $I(2R\,d\theta)B$ is balanced by inward components of wire tension $2T\sin(d\theta) \approx 2T\,d\theta \implies \boxed{T = I B R}$!

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Why Doubling Turns $N$ in a Galvanometer Doubles Current Sensitivity $S_I$ But Does NOT Change Voltage Sensitivity $S_V$!): If you double the number of turns ($N \to 2N$) using the same gauge of wire, the length of wire also doubles, so coil resistance doubles ($R_G \to 2R_G$)! Therefore, $S_I = \frac{NAB}{k}$ doubles, whereas $S_V = \frac{NAB}{k R_G}$ remains unchanged!
  • Trap 2 (Opposite Rule for Parallel Charges vs. Parallel Wires!): Two like static charges ($+q, +q$) repel, whereas two parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction ATTRACT! Wait: what about two parallel beams of electrons moving side-by-side at speed $v$? They have electrostatic repulsion $F_e$ AND magnetic attraction $F_m = F_e(v^2/c^2)$, so since $v < c$, two parallel electron beams in the lab frame still have a net repulsion $F_{\text{net}} = F_e(1 - v^2/c^2)$!

conclusion: You have mastered Chapter 18: Moving Charges & Magnetism! Next, in Chapter 19, we explore permanent magnets, Earth's magnetic field, and magnetic materials.
summary:
• Biot-Savart: $d\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I(d\vec{\ell}\times\hat{r})}{r^2}$; Straight wire $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}(\sin\theta_1 + \sin\theta_2)$; Arc $B = \frac{\mu_0 I\alpha}{4\pi R}$; Axis of coil $B = \frac{\mu_0 NIR^2}{2(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}}$.
  • Ampere's Law: $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = \mu_0 I_{\text{enc}}$; Solenoid $B = \mu_0 n I$ (end $= \frac{1}{2}\mu_0 nI$); Solid cylinder inside $B = \frac{\mu_0 Ir}{2\pi R^2}$.
  • Lorentz Force: $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$, $R = \frac{mv}{qB} = \frac{\sqrt{2mK}}{qB}$, $T = \frac{2\pi m}{qB}$ (independent of $v$).
  • Wires & Dipoles: $\vec{F} = I(\vec{L}_{\text{eff}}\times\vec{B})$, $\frac{F}{L} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$; $\vec{\mu} = NIA$, $\frac{\mu}{L} = \frac{q}{2m}$, $\vec{\tau} = \vec{\mu}\times\vec{B}$.

questions.prompt: A wire carrying a current of $I = 10\text{ A}$ is bent into the shape of a regular square loop of side length $a = 20\text{ cm}$. What is the magnitude of the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ at the geometric center of the square? ($\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}$)
questions.explanation: Each of the 4 sides is at perpendicular distance $d = a/2 = 0.10\text{ m}$ from the center and subtends $\theta_1 = \theta_2 = 45^\circ$. Thus $B = 4 \times \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi (a/2)}(\sin 45^\circ + \sin 45^\circ) = \frac{2\sqrt{2}\mu_0 I}{\pi a} = 4 \times \frac{10^{-7} \times 10}{0.10}\left(\sqrt{2}\right) = 4\sqrt{2} \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}$.

questions.prompt: A proton ($m_p, +e$) and an alpha particle ($4m_p, +2e$) enter a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ perpendicularly with the exact same kinetic energy $K$. What is the ratio of the radii of their circular paths ($R_p : R_\alpha$)?
questions.explanation: Using $R = \frac{\sqrt{2mK}}{qB}$, at the same $K$ and $B$ we have $R \propto \frac{\sqrt{m}}{q}$. Therefore, $\frac{R_p}{R_\alpha} = \frac{\sqrt{m_p}/e}{\sqrt{4m_p}/(2e)} = \frac{1}{2/2} = 1 : 1$!

questions.prompt: A long straight wire of radius $R$ carries a steady current $I$ uniformly distributed across its circular cross-section. The ratio of the magnetic field at radial distance $r_1 = \frac{R}{2}$ (inside the wire) to that at radial distance $r_2 = 2R$ (outside the wire) is:
questions.explanation: Inside ($r_1 = R/2$): $B_{\text{in}} = \frac{\mu_0 I r_1}{2\pi R^2} = \frac{\mu_0 I (R/2)}{2\pi R^2} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R}$. Outside ($r_2 = 2R$): $B_{\text{out}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r_2} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi(2R)} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R}$. Therefore, the ratio $B_{\text{in}} : B_{\text{out}} = 1 : 1$!

questions.prompt: A circular coil of radius $R$ carries an electric current $I$. At what axial distance $x$ from the center of the coil does the magnetic field drop to $\frac{1}{8}$ of its value at the center?
questions.explanation: Since $\frac{B_{\text{center}}}{B_{\text{axis}}} = \left(1 + \frac{x^2}{R^2}\right)^{3/2} = 8 = 2^3$, taking the $2/3$ power gives $1 + \frac{x^2}{R^2} = 2^2 = 4 \implies x^2 = 3R^2 \implies x = \sqrt{3}\,R$.

questions.prompt: A semicircular wire of radius $R = 10\text{ cm}$ carrying current $I = 5\text{ A}$ lies in the xy-plane inside a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B} = 0.4\,\hat{k}\text{ T}$ perpendicular to the plane. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force acting on the semicircular wire?
questions.explanation: In a uniform magnetic field, the effective length of a semicircle of radius $R$ is the straight diameter joining its two endpoints: $L_{\text{eff}} = 2R = 2(0.10\text{ m}) = 0.20\text{ m}$. Thus $F = I L_{\text{eff}} B = (5\text{ A})(0.20\text{ m})(0.4\text{ T}) = 0.4\text{ N}$.

questions.prompt: A thin non-conducting circular disk of radius $R$ carries a uniform surface charge $+q$ and rotates with angular speed $\omega$ about its central perpendicular axis. What is the magnetic dipole moment $\mu$ of the rotating disk?
questions.explanation: Using the Universal Gyromagnetic Ratio $\frac{\mu}{L} = \frac{q}{2m}$ with the moment of inertia of a solid disk $I_{\text{MI}} = \frac{1}{2}mR^2$: $\mu = \frac{q}{2m}(I_{\text{MI}}\omega) = \frac{q}{2m}\left(\frac{1}{2}mR^2\omega\right) = \frac{1}{4}q\omega R^2$.

questions.prompt: A particle of mass $m$ and charge $+q$ enters with speed $v$ perpendicularly into a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ confined to a strip of width $d = \frac{mv}{2qB}$. By what angle $\theta$ is the velocity vector of the particle deflected when it emerges from the opposite boundary of the strip?
questions.explanation: The radius of the circular arc inside the field is $R = \frac{mv}{qB}$. Since strip width is $d = \frac{R}{2}$, the angle of deflection satisfies $\sin\theta = \frac{d}{R} = \frac{1}{2} \implies \theta = 30^\circ$.

questions.prompt: A long cylindrical conductor of radius $R$ carries a uniform current density $\vec{J} = J\hat{k}$ along its axis. A cylindrical cavity of radius $R/2$ is bored parallel to the axis such that the distance between the cylinder axis and the cavity axis is $d$. What is the magnitude of the magnetic field at any point inside the empty cavity?
options: Varies with distance from cavity center
questions.explanation: By Ampere's law superposition ($\vec{B}_{\text{cavity}} = \frac{1}{2}\mu_0(\vec{J} \times \vec{d})$), the magnetic field inside the off-center cylindrical cavity is strictly uniform everywhere and has magnitude $B = \frac{1}{2}\mu_0 J d$.
